frameworks.name: Three Things to Win Framework
frameworks.definition: Success requires three elements: the courage to start, the intelligence to learn continuously, and the heart to persist—all of which you already possess.

frameworks.name: Information Paralysis vs. Action Gap
frameworks.definition: Most people know what to do but delay action by seeking a perfect plan; the real world rewards starting imperfectly and learning via feedback rather than pre-planning.

frameworks.name: School vs. Real World Learning Model
frameworks.definition: School provides clear directions, single correct answers, and immediate feedback; the real world offers many right paths, only one wrong path (inaction), and delayed feedback—requiring a behavioral reorientation.

claims.text: You already know what to do to achieve most goals; you delay action by seeking the perfect plan when the plan will change as soon as you receive new information anyway (Alex Hormozi).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Perfect-plan-seeking is a guilt-free procrastination mechanism disguised as diligence.
bounded_by: Does not apply when foundational knowledge is completely absent (e.g., building a nuclear reactor).
Does not excuse recklessness or safety-critical decisions.

claims.text: The foundational skill that overshadows all others is the ability to delay gratification—to defer a moment of reward long enough that a first external feedback loop (sale, lead, follower) arrives and reinforces continued effort (Alex Hormozi).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Delaying gratification extends your runway until the first external feedback arrives; that feedback is psychologically outsized and strong enough to shift from willpower-driven effort to intrinsic motivation ('oh, this could work').
bounded_by: Does not apply to scenarios where feedback is impossible (e.g., a one-time event with no iteration).

claims.text: Personal excellence is the ultimate rebellion against systems designed to capture your attention and prevent action; if you want to compete against those systems, be great and do it for yourself (Alex Hormozi, citing Andy Frisella).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Competing for attention in an attention economy
claims.mechanism: Excellence is a form of active resistance against entropy and distraction; most people default to mediocrity because the systems pulling them toward inaction are stronger than their willpower, so excellence requires sustained, deliberate effort.

anchors.value: hundreds of billions of dollars per day

claims.text: Entertainment consumption (social media, porn, alcohol, clubs, motivation porn) directly prevents action on your most important goals because every dollar and minute of attention you give to entertainment is time you are not spending on the outcome that matters (Alex Hormozi).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Goals that require sustained action over time
claims.mechanism: Attention is zero-sum; entertainment is engineered to capture it. Each minute spent on entertainment is a minute not spent on your goal, and the opportunity cost is invisible until you compare the two outcomes side by side.
bounded_by: Does not forbid all entertainment; the issue is the total attention budget, not the category.

claims.text: If you perceive time passing slowly (as younger people do), you must over-index on patience and delayed gratification, because your perception of time will naturally speed up as you age (Alex Hormozi).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Age < 30 or perception of time moving slowly
claims.mechanism: Older people exhibit more patience not because they are psychologically different, but because one year at age 40 is a smaller percentage of their life than one year at age 20. Your patience capacity may not change, but the time interval will eventually feel shorter.

numbers.axis: perceived duration as percentage of life

claims.text: The real world differs fundamentally from school: school has clear directions, one correct answer, and immediate feedback; the real world has many right answers, only one wrong answer (inaction), and delayed feedback—beginners are paralyzed because they assume real-world decisions have only one right answer like school (Alex Hormozi).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Transitioning from formal education to business/independent work
claims.mechanism: School trains the brain to fear any deviation from the single correct answer; when confronted with multiple viable paths in the real world, the absence of a guaranteed answer paralyzes decision-making.
bounded_by: Does not apply to domains with single correct answers (mathematics, safety-critical systems).

claims.text: Most goals that matter (getting in shape, building a business, acquiring a skill) have a known path to success that requires only action, yet people delay by researching the 'best' program, 'best' diet, or 'best' strategy when starting imperfectly and iterating is faster than perfect planning (Alex Hormozi).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Goal path is already known from domain common sense
Perfect execution is not required for first feedback loop
claims.mechanism: The cost of delay (time lost) exceeds the cost of imperfection (course correction); iteration based on real-world feedback converges faster than pre-planning based on imagined scenarios.
bounded_by: Does not apply when the path is unknown or when initial conditions are safety-critical.

claims.text: A person who dedicates 50 years to one activity with continuous improvement becomes incredibly successful, yet most people do not do this; the barrier is distraction (internal and external), not impossibility (Alex Hormozi).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Success is mechanically straightforward (do one thing, get better at it); the mechanism is not novel, but distraction prevents execution.

claims.text: When asked whether you would sign a contract guaranteeing millionaire status in 10 years but zero real money until then, nearly every person says yes, yet this reveals that most people intellectually understand delayed gratification but fail to execute it in practice (Alex Hormozi).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: The contract eliminates uncertainty and risk, which makes delayed gratification acceptable; in real business, uncertainty is present, which is why most people fail to delay reward despite intellectually accepting the principle.

numbers.axis: percentage of people willing to commit

anchors.region: actual uncertain business path requiring 5-10 years

claims.text: Suffering from social disapproval (losing friendships, not being perceived as cool, not appearing at social events, not wearing brand-name clothes) is a real cost that will occur when you prioritize goals over fitting in—the question is whether a lifetime of mediocrity is worth avoiding that suffering (Alex Hormozi).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Goal requires visible sacrifice of social status
You are in a social circle that does not share your goal
claims.mechanism: The comparison is not 'suffering vs. no suffering' but 'this suffering vs. the crushing feeling of mediocrity for the rest of your life'—reframing it this way makes the choice clearer.
bounded_by: Does not prescribe isolation for all relationships; selective sacrifice, not total severance, is the real move.

claims.text: Many right paths exist to an outcome, but only one thing prevents you from achieving any of them: fear—fear of failure, fear of disapproval, and fear of social cost (Alex Hormozi).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Fear is the only universal constraint; remove fear and multiple paths become visible and executable.
bounded_by: Does not eliminate other constraints (capital, knowledge, talent), only the psychological constraint of fear.

examples.text: If asked to guess how to get in shape without looking up programs or diets, most people say 'go to the gym, do weights and cardio, eat more protein and less junk food.' They already know the path; they delay by researching the 'best' program. Similarly, most people know they should start a business, get better at their craft, or move toward their goal—they already know what to do, but they seek the perfect plan instead of starting imperfectly.

A young team member asked the speaker 'What's my next career move?' after only 30 days on the job. The speaker responded: 'Give it a second. You still suck. You went from suck to proficient. You're not great yet. Calm down.' This illustrates that beginners underestimate how long competence takes and overestimate their readiness for the next rung.

The speaker knew two billionaire CEOs: one took his company public and made all his money there; the other took his company public, found it was a mess, took it private, and now does only private deals—and is actually richer. Both gave conflicting advice about going public, yet both succeeded. This shows there are many right paths, not one correct answer. The only wrong path is fear and inaction.

practices.text: Give yourself permission to start in a role that is not your endgame; see it as one tile in the larger painting of your career—e.g., starting in door-to-door sales or cold calling as foundational experience even though you know those are not your final destination.

Use the goal-frame filter: when deciding whether to attend a social event or invest time in a relationship, ask 'Does this increase or decrease the likelihood I achieve my goal?' If it decreases likelihood, decline; if it increases likelihood, attend.

Over-index on patience and delayed gratification when you are young (age < 30) because your perception of time moving slowly is temporary—time will eventually speed up as you age, and your patience capacity will naturally increase.
